2007.us: Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone in January, and it went on sale in June. By spring, subprime mortgage lenders were going bankrupt, an early sign of the coming financial crisis.
2007.latam: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner was elected president of Argentina, succeeding her husband Néstor. In December, Venezuelan voters narrowly rejected Hugo Chávez’s constitutional reform, his first defeat at the polls.
2007.europe: Nicolas Sarkozy won France’s presidency, and Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair as British prime minister. In September, savers queued outside Northern Rock in Britain’s first bank run in over a century.
2007.russia: Vladimir Putin, barred from a third straight term, named Dmitry Medvedev as his preferred successor in December. Sochi won the 2014 Winter Olympics, and Boris Yeltsin died in April.
2007.mideast: Hamas seized control of Gaza from rival Fatah in June, splitting Palestinian rule in two. In Iraq, the US sent more than 20,000 extra troops in a “surge” against sectarian violence.
2007.africa: Kenya’s December election ended in disputed results and deadly unrest after Mwai Kibaki was declared the winner over Raila Odinga. Nigeria saw its first handover between elected civilian presidents.
2007.india: Former Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto was assassinated at a rally in December. India won cricket’s first T20 World Cup, and Pratibha Patil became its first woman president.
2007.china: Xi Jinping joined the Communist Party’s top leadership in October as Beijing prepared for the Olympics. Japan’s Shinzo Abe resigned after a year, and South Korea elected Lee Myung-bak.

2008.us: Lehman Brothers collapsed in September, turning a housing slump into a global financial crisis. In November, Barack Obama was elected the first Black president of the United States.
2008.latam: Fidel Castro formally handed Cuba’s presidency to his brother Raúl in February. In July, Colombia’s army tricked FARC rebels into freeing Ingrid Betancourt and 14 other hostages without a shot fired.
2008.europe: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in February. In October, Iceland’s three biggest banks collapsed within a week, and governments across Europe rushed to rescue their lenders.
2008.russia: Dmitry Medvedev became president, with Vladimir Putin as prime minister. In August, Russia fought a five-day war with Georgia, then recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent.
2008.mideast: Iraq and the US agreed in November that American troops would leave by the end of 2011. On December 27, Israel launched a major offensive against Hamas in Gaza after rocket fire.
2008.africa: After more than 1,000 deaths, Kenya’s rivals agreed to share power in February. Zimbabwe sank into crisis with a disputed election, runaway inflation and a cholera outbreak.
2008.india: Ten gunmen attacked hotels, a train station and other sites in Mumbai in November, killing 166 people. Earlier, India launched its first Moon probe, and the Indian Premier League began.
2008.china: A May earthquake in Sichuan killed nearly 70,000 people. In August, Beijing hosted the Summer Olympics, and China topped the gold medal table for the first time.

2011.us: US Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden in May. Standard & Poor’s downgraded US government debt in August, and Occupy Wall Street protesters camped in lower Manhattan from September.
2011.latam: Dilma Rousseff took office as Brazil’s first woman president. Chilean students held months of mass protests for free public education, and Hugo Chávez revealed he was being treated for cancer.
2011.europe: The euro debt crisis pushed Portugal into a bailout and toppled leaders in Greece and Italy. In July, a far-right extremist killed 77 people in Norway, most at a youth camp.
2011.russia: In September, Vladimir Putin announced he would return to the presidency, swapping jobs with Dmitry Medvedev. After December’s parliamentary election, tens of thousands protested in Moscow over alleged vote fraud.
2011.mideast: The Arab Spring toppled Tunisia’s Ben Ali in January and Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak in February. Libya’s Muammar Gaddafi was killed in October, and Syria’s protests grew into an armed uprising.
2011.africa: South Sudan became the world’s newest country on July 9. Famine struck parts of Somalia, and Ivory Coast’s Laurent Gbagbo was arrested after refusing to accept his election defeat.
2011.india: India won the Cricket World Cup at home in April, and Anna Hazare’s hunger strikes against corruption drew huge crowds. In May, US forces killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan.
2011.china: On March 11, a magnitude 9 earthquake and tsunami left about 18,000 dead or missing in Japan and caused meltdowns at Fukushima. North Korea’s Kim Jong-il died in December.

2014.us: Protests erupted in Ferguson, Missouri, after a police officer shot dead Michael Brown, an unarmed Black teenager, in August. That summer, the Ice Bucket Challenge swept social media.
2014.latam: Brazil hosted the World Cup and lost its semifinal 7-1 to Germany. In Mexico, 43 students from Ayotzinapa disappeared in September, and in December the US and Cuba agreed to restore ties.
2014.europe: Ukraine’s president fled in February after months of protests in Kyiv, and war broke out in the east. In September, Scotland voted 55 to 45 percent to stay in the United Kingdom.
2014.russia: Russia hosted the Winter Olympics in Sochi, then annexed Crimea from Ukraine in March. Western sanctions and falling oil prices sent the ruble crashing by December.
2014.mideast: Islamic State seized Mosul in June and declared a caliphate across parts of Iraq and Syria. That summer, a 50-day war between Israel and Hamas killed over 2,200 Palestinians and 73 Israelis.
2014.africa: Ebola spread through Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone in the worst outbreak on record. In Nigeria, Boko Haram kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, sparking the #BringBackOurGirls campaign.
2014.india: Narendra Modi led the BJP to a landslide election win in May. India’s Mangalyaan probe reached Mars orbit on its first attempt, and Malala Yousafzai shared the Nobel Peace Prize.
2014.china: Pro-democracy protesters occupied Hong Kong streets for 79 days in the Umbrella Movement. In April, South Korea’s Sewol ferry sank, killing 304 people, most of them high school students.

2015.us: In June, the Supreme Court ruled same-sex couples have the right to marry nationwide. That month, a gunman killed nine Black worshippers at a Charleston church, and Donald Trump launched his campaign.
2015.latam: Zika virus spread across Brazil and was linked to a surge in babies born with small heads. Drug lord El Chapo escaped a Mexican prison through a mile-long tunnel in July.
2015.europe: More than a million refugees and migrants reached Europe, many fleeing Syria’s war. Paris suffered the Charlie Hebdo attack in January and coordinated attacks that killed 130 people in November.
2015.russia: Opposition politician Boris Nemtsov was shot dead near the Kremlin in February. In September, Russia began airstrikes in Syria in support of Bashar al-Assad’s government.
2015.mideast: Iran agreed in July to limit its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief. In March, Saudi Arabia under new King Salman began leading airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen.
2015.africa: Muhammadu Buhari became the first opposition candidate to unseat a sitting president in Nigeria. In April, al-Shabaab gunmen killed 148 people at Garissa University College in Kenya.
2015.india: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck Nepal in April, killing nearly 9,000 people. In India, Arvind Kejriwal’s young Aam Aadmi Party won 67 of 70 seats in Delhi’s election.
2015.china: China’s stock market crashed in the summer, and in October Beijing announced the end of its one-child policy. In August, chemical explosions at Tianjin’s port killed 173 people.

2016.us: Donald Trump won the presidency in November, beating Hillary Clinton in the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. In June, a gunman killed 49 people at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando.
2016.latam: Rio de Janeiro hosted the Olympics, and Brazil’s Senate removed Dilma Rousseff in August. Colombia signed a peace deal with FARC rebels, and Fidel Castro died in November.
2016.europe: Britain voted 52 to 48 percent in June to leave the European Union. Terror attacks hit Brussels, Nice and Berlin, and Portugal won the Euro 2016 football championship.
2016.russia: The McLaren report described state-backed doping of Russian athletes, and Russia’s track team missed the Rio Olympics. US intelligence accused Russia of election interference, which Moscow denied.
2016.mideast: A failed military coup in Turkey in July was followed by mass arrests under President Erdoğan. In December, Syrian government forces backed by Russia retook all of Aleppo.
2016.africa: In the Gambia, Yahya Jammeh lost the December election after 22 years in power, then refused to step down. Ethiopia declared a state of emergency after months of protests.
2016.india: On November 8, Narendra Modi abruptly withdrew 500 and 1,000 rupee notes, about 86 percent of the cash in circulation. Long queues formed outside banks for weeks.
2016.china: Google’s AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul in March. Huge candlelight protests led South Korea’s parliament to impeach President Park Geun-hye in December.

2017.us: Donald Trump took office in January, and millions joined Women’s Marches the next day. Hurricane Harvey flooded Houston in August, and in October the #MeToo movement spread online.
2017.latam: Months of protests against Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela left more than 120 dead. In September, an earthquake killed about 370 people in Mexico, and Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico.
2017.europe: Emmanuel Macron was elected president of France at 39. In June, the Grenfell Tower fire in London killed 72 people, and in October Catalonia held a banned independence referendum.
2017.russia: Alexei Navalny’s video alleging corruption by Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev sparked nationwide protests in March. In December, the IOC barred Russia’s team from the 2018 Winter Olympics over doping.
2017.mideast: Iraqi forces retook Mosul from Islamic State in July, and Raqqa fell in October. Mohammed bin Salman became Saudi crown prince, and Saudi Arabia and its allies cut ties with Qatar.
2017.africa: Robert Mugabe resigned in November after 37 years in power, following a military takeover in Zimbabwe. In September, Kenya’s Supreme Court annulled the presidential election, a first in Africa.
2017.india: India launched a nationwide goods and services tax on July 1, replacing many state levies. From August, more than 600,000 Rohingya refugees fled Myanmar into Bangladesh.
2017.china: North Korea tested long-range missiles and its most powerful nuclear bomb. South Korea removed Park Geun-hye from office, and China’s Communist Party wrote “Xi Jinping Thought” into its constitution.

2018.us: After a gunman killed 17 people at a high school in Parkland, Florida, students led nationwide marches. A US-China trade war began with rising tariffs, and Democrats won the House in November.
2018.latam: Andrés Manuel López Obrador won Mexico’s presidency in July, and Jair Bolsonaro won Brazil’s in October. Millions of Venezuelans had fled economic collapse, many to Colombia and Peru.
2018.europe: Yellow vest protests against fuel taxes spread across France from November. In May, the EU’s GDPR privacy rules took effect, flooding inboxes with consent emails.
2018.russia: Vladimir Putin won a fourth term in March, and Russia hosted the football World Cup that summer. Britain blamed Russia for poisoning ex-spy Sergei Skripal with a nerve agent, which Moscow denied.
2018.mideast: The US quit the Iran nuclear deal and moved its embassy to Jerusalem in May. Saudi women began driving legally, and journalist Jamal Khashoggi was killed in Saudi Arabia’s Istanbul consulate.
2018.africa: Abiy Ahmed became Ethiopia’s prime minister in April and made peace with Eritrea after two decades of hostility. In South Africa, Cyril Ramaphosa replaced Jacob Zuma as president.
2018.india: India’s Supreme Court decriminalized gay sex in September, and the 182-meter Statue of Unity became the world’s tallest statue. In Pakistan, former cricket star Imran Khan became prime minister.
2018.china: China removed presidential term limits in March, allowing Xi Jinping to stay on indefinitely. In June, Kim Jong-un and Donald Trump held the first North Korea-US summit, in Singapore.

2019.us: The longest government shutdown so far, 35 days, ended in January. Robert Mueller’s Russia report came out in April, and in December the House impeached Donald Trump over his dealings with Ukraine.
2019.latam: A subway fare rise in Chile sparked mass protests in October. Bolivia’s Evo Morales resigned in November amid protests over a disputed election, and fires in the Amazon drew global alarm.
2019.europe: Fire destroyed Notre-Dame’s roof and spire in April. Boris Johnson became British prime minister in July and won a large majority in December, promising to “get Brexit done.”
2019.russia: Large protests broke out in Moscow in the summer after opposition candidates were barred from city elections. In December, the World Anti-Doping Agency banned Russia from major sporting events for four years.
2019.mideast: Mass protests forced out Algeria’s Abdelaziz Bouteflika in April and broke out in Lebanon and Iraq in October. Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi died during a US raid in Syria.
2019.africa: After months of protests, Sudan’s army removed Omar al-Bashir in April after 30 years in power. Cyclone Idai killed more than 1,000 people in Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi.
2019.india: Narendra Modi won a bigger majority in May. In August, his government revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s special status, and a new citizenship law set off nationwide protests in December.
2019.china: Huge crowds marched in Hong Kong from June against an extradition bill, starting months of clashes. Naruhito became Japan’s emperor in May, and a new pneumonia appeared in Wuhan in December.

2020.us: COVID-19 shut down much of the country from March. After a Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd in May, protests spread nationwide, and Joe Biden won the presidency in November.
2020.latam: COVID-19 hit Brazil, Mexico and Peru especially hard. In October, Chileans voted 78 percent in favor of writing a new constitution, and Argentina legalized abortion in December.
2020.europe: Britain formally left the EU on January 31. In March, Italy imposed Europe’s first national COVID-19 lockdown, and Belarus erupted in protests after a disputed August election.
2020.russia: Voters approved constitutional changes in July that could let Vladimir Putin stay in power until 2036. In August, Alexei Navalny was poisoned with a nerve agent; the Kremlin denied involvement.
2020.mideast: A US drone strike killed Iranian general Qassem Soleimani in January. In August, an explosion at Beirut’s port killed more than 200 people, and the UAE and Bahrain normalized ties with Israel.
2020.africa: War broke out in Ethiopia’s Tigray region in November. In October, #EndSARS protests against police brutality swept Nigeria, and in August Mali’s military ousted its president.
2020.india: India’s sudden COVID-19 lockdown in March sent millions of migrant workers walking home. In June, 20 Indian soldiers died in a clash with Chinese troops in the Himalayas.
2020.china: China locked down Wuhan in January as the new coronavirus spread. In June, Beijing imposed a national security law on Hong Kong, and the Tokyo Olympics were postponed by a year.

2021.us: Supporters of Donald Trump stormed the Capitol on January 6 as Congress certified Joe Biden’s win. In August, US troops left Afghanistan after a chaotic airlift from Kabul.
2021.latam: Haiti’s president Jovenel Moïse was assassinated at home in July. Days later, Cubans staged the largest anti-government protests in decades, and El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in September.
2021.europe: Floods in Germany and Belgium killed more than 200 people in July. Angela Merkel stepped down after 16 years as German chancellor, and Olaf Scholz took over in December.
2021.russia: Alexei Navalny was arrested on returning to Russia in January, sparking nationwide protests. By December, Russia had massed troops near Ukraine and demanded that NATO stop expanding east.
2021.mideast: The giant ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for six days in March. In May, an 11-day Israel-Hamas war killed more than 250 people, most of them in Gaza.
2021.africa: Riots after Jacob Zuma was jailed left about 350 dead in South Africa in July. Soldiers seized power in Guinea and Sudan, and the war in Ethiopia’s Tigray region spread.
2021.india: A Delta variant wave overwhelmed India’s hospitals in spring, and oxygen ran short. The Taliban took Kabul in August, and Narendra Modi repealed his farm laws after a year of protests.
2021.china: Tokyo held the delayed Olympics in July with almost no spectators. South Korea’s Squid Game became Netflix’s most-watched series, and China’s property giant Evergrande defaulted on its debts.

2022.us: The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in June, ending the national right to abortion. Inflation hit 9.1 percent, a 40-year high, and OpenAI released ChatGPT in November.
2022.latam: Lula narrowly beat Jair Bolsonaro in October to win back Brazil’s presidency. Gustavo Petro became Colombia’s first leftist president, and Lionel Messi led Argentina to World Cup victory in December.
2022.europe: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February sent millions of refugees west and energy prices soaring. Queen Elizabeth II died in September, and Britain had three prime ministers in one year.
2022.russia: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, and Western sanctions followed. A September call-up of 300,000 reservists sent many Russian men fleeing abroad.
2022.mideast: Protests swept Iran after 22-year-old Mahsa Amini died in morality police custody in September. Qatar hosted the first World Cup in the Arab world, and Benjamin Netanyahu won back power in Israel.
2022.africa: Ethiopia’s government and Tigrayan forces signed a peace deal in November, ending two years of war. William Ruto won Kenya’s presidency, and East Africa suffered its worst drought in 40 years.
2022.india: Sri Lanka’s economic collapse drove protesters into the president’s house, and Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled in July. Floods covered about a third of Pakistan in late summer, killing more than 1,700 people.
2022.china: Former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe was shot dead in July. Xi Jinping secured a third term in October, and after rare protests in November, China abruptly ended its zero-COVID policy.

2023.us: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in March, setting off a brief banking scare. Donald Trump was indicted in four criminal cases, and Hollywood writers and actors went on strike for months.
2023.latam: On January 8, supporters of Jair Bolsonaro stormed Brazil’s Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace. In November, Argentines elected Javier Milei, a libertarian who campaigned with a chainsaw to symbolize spending cuts.
2023.europe: Finland joined NATO in April, and King Charles III was crowned in May. In France, President Emmanuel Macron raised the retirement age from 62 to 64 despite months of mass protests.
2023.russia: The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin in March. In June, Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin led a brief mutiny, and in August he died in a plane crash.
2023.mideast: Earthquakes in Turkey and Syria killed more than 50,000 people in February. On October 7, Hamas-led attacks killed about 1,200 people in Israel, and Israel launched a war in Gaza.
2023.africa: War broke out in Sudan in April between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, displacing millions. Soldiers seized power in Niger in July and in Gabon in August.
2023.india: India passed China as the world’s most populous country, by UN estimates. In August, Chandrayaan-3 made the first landing near the Moon’s south pole, and New Delhi hosted the G20 in September.
2023.china: China reopened its borders in January after three years of zero-COVID rules. In August, Japan began releasing treated water from the Fukushima plant, and China banned Japanese seafood in response.

2024.us: Donald Trump survived an assassination attempt in July, and Joe Biden ended his reelection bid days later. Trump then defeated Kamala Harris in November to win a second, non-consecutive term.
2024.latam: Claudia Sheinbaum was elected Mexico’s first woman president in June. In Venezuela, electoral authorities declared Nicolás Maduro the winner in July, while the opposition published tallies showing its candidate had won.
2024.europe: Paris hosted the Summer Olympics, and Labour’s July landslide made Keir Starmer British prime minister. In October, flash floods around Valencia, Spain, killed more than 220 people.
2024.russia: Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in February, and Vladimir Putin won a fifth term in March. Days later, gunmen killed more than 140 people at Crocus City Hall near Moscow.
2024.mideast: Israel’s war in Gaza spread to Lebanon, where an Israeli strike killed Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in September. In December, rebels swept into Damascus and Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia.
2024.africa: Young Kenyans protested a tax-raising finance bill in June, briefly storming parliament. In South Africa, the ANC lost its majority for the first time since 1994 and formed a coalition government.
2024.india: Narendra Modi won a third term in June, though his BJP lost its outright majority. In August, student-led protests forced Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee to India.
2024.china: Taiwan elected Lai Ching-te president in January. On December 3, South Korea’s President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law; lawmakers voted it down within hours and later impeached him.

2025.us: Wildfires tore through Los Angeles in January as Donald Trump began his second term. His sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs shook markets in April, and a 43-day government shutdown became the longest ever.
2025.latam: Brazil’s Supreme Court sentenced Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years for plotting a coup, which he denies. Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize in October.
2025.europe: On April 28, a blackout cut power across Spain and Portugal for hours. Pope Francis had died a week earlier, and in May, Leo XIV became the first American pope.
2025.russia: In June, Ukrainian drones hidden in trucks struck bomber bases deep inside Russia. In August, Vladimir Putin met Donald Trump in Alaska, without a deal to end the war.
2025.mideast: Israel and Iran fought a 12-day war in June, and US bombers struck Iranian nuclear sites. In October, a US-brokered Gaza ceasefire freed the last living hostages and nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners.
2025.africa: M23 rebels seized Goma and Bukavu in eastern Congo early in the year. In October, Sudan’s RSF captured El Fasher after an 18-month siege, amid reports of mass killings.
2025.india: After gunmen killed 26 people in Kashmir in April, India and Pakistan fought four days of missile and drone strikes in May. Youth-led protests toppled Nepal’s government in September.
2025.china: Chinese startup DeepSeek’s low-cost AI model jolted tech stocks in January. South Korea’s top court removed Yoon Suk Yeol in April, and Sanae Takaichi became Japan’s first woman prime minister in October.
